observation_summary: The DateUtils.truncate method fails during DST transitions because it relies on Calendar.set() operations that trigger time-zone-aware recalculations, leading to an incorrect hour shift.
hypothesis: The DateUtils.truncate method incorrectly uses Calendar.set() operations to truncate time fields, which triggers internal Calendar recalculations that are sensitive to Daylight Saving Time (DST) transitions. When truncating during a DST switch, these recalculations shift the time by an hour, causing the observed mismatch between MDT and MST.
prediction: The fix will involve bypassing the standard Calendar.set() methods for lower-level time fields (milliseconds, seconds, minutes) and instead performing direct arithmetic on the underlying long timestamp to avoid triggering the DST-sensitive Calendar logic.
experiment_rationale: The provided fix diff clearly shows the implementation of manual arithmetic on the long timestamp to replace the problematic Calendar.set() calls, confirming that the original procedural approach was flawed for DST-sensitive calculations.
reasoning_summary: The bug is a classic case of an incorrect algorithmic approach to time manipulation. Using Calendar.set() is not idempotent or safe when DST transitions occur because the Calendar object attempts to 'fix' the time based on the local timezone rules. The fix replaces this with direct long-integer arithmetic, which is the correct way to perform truncation without triggering side effects.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The issue is not a missing guard or validation, but an incorrect implementation of the truncation logic itself.
The issue is not about setting a variable to the wrong value, but about the procedural logic used to calculate the truncated time.
